headline_en: 18,000 workers will go to Malaysia in phases: Expatriates' Welfare Secretary
summary_en: On 22 January 2025, after workers who had missed the 31 May 2024 Malaysia entry deadline blocked Karwan Bazar and sat in front of the ministry, Expatriates' Welfare Secretary Md. Ruhul Amin said talks with Malaysia were progressing and 18,000 workers would go in phases. He said Malaysia had agreed in principle, the method was not yet fixed, and recruiting agencies had refunded 81 percent of the workers' money. The article recaps that 16,970 workers with final clearance could not travel by the deadline (protesters say 18,000).

facts.statement: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Secretary Md. Ruhul Amin said on 22 January 2025 that there was positive progress on sending to Malaysia the workers who had been unable to go, that the sending process could be finalised very soon, and that 18,000 workers would go to Malaysia in phases.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare Secretary Md. Ruhul Amin

facts.statement: The secretary said the ministry was working both on sending to Malaysia those who could not go and on getting their money refunded by the recruiting agencies.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare Secretary Md. Ruhul Amin

facts.statement: The technical committee of the Bangladesh High Commission in Malaysia and the technical committee of Malaysia's Home Ministry had already met twice (described as fruitful, with progress); another meeting was due in February 2025; Malaysia had agreed in principle and the secretary hoped the matter would be final by April 2025.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare Secretary Md. Ruhul Amin

facts.statement: The list of the workers had been sent to Malaysia; discussions had begun and were continuing but the method was not yet fixed; the proposals were to be discussed at minister level in Malaysia, and the secretary said that once Malaysia decided, sending workers would start within 15 days. Workers would be informed once the process was final.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare Secretary Md. Ruhul Amin

facts.statement: The secretary said efforts were being made so that the stranded Malaysia-bound workers would not face a new burden of costs in order to go.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare Secretary Md. Ruhul Amin

facts.statement: After Malaysia's labour market last opened in 2022, a syndicate was accused of controlling the market; amid wide criticism and various international pressure Malaysia stopped taking foreign workers, having first set 31 May 2024 as the deadline for workers to enter.

16,970 Bangladeshi workers who had completed every step and held final clearance could not get to Malaysia by the 31 May 2024 deadline; the protesting workers claim the number is 18,000. The government had promised to recover these workers' money from the recruiting agencies.
facts.source_in_article: reporter's background; protesters for the 18,000 figure

facts.statement: As of two days before 22 January 2025, recruiting agencies had refunded the money of 81 percent of the workers who could not go to Malaysia, and had submitted lists with the workers' signatures to the ministry.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare Secretary Md. Ruhul Amin

facts.statement: Recruiting agencies had been given a deadline of Thursday 23 January 2025 to pay back the money of workers who could not go to Malaysia; the secretary said action would be taken against those that did not refund.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare Secretary Md. Ruhul Amin

facts.statement: About a hundred workers who had been unable to go to Malaysia, some wearing burial shrouds, blocked one side of the SAARC Fountain intersection at Karwan Bazar, Dhaka from 9 am on 22 January 2025 chanting against the syndicate and demanding to go to Malaysia and to meet the Chief Adviser; police moved them aside at about 11 to 11:15 am (the article gives both times).

The protesting workers then marched to the road in front of Probashi Kalyan Bhaban (the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry) at about 12:30 pm; at police request a four-member delegation went into the ministry at about 1:30 pm and officials sat with them at about 2:30 pm; protesters were still on the road chanting at 3 pm.

Asked about talks with the protesters, the secretary said progress had been conveyed to the workers through the media and they would be told directly if they came, adding: the workers do not want a syndicate, you do not, and we do not either.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare Secretary Md. Ruhul Amin

headline_en: Jordan to take 250 women workers through BOESL, with medical care and airfare
summary_en: A September 2024 recruitment notice: state-owned Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) will recruit 250 experienced women machine operators for Tasker Apparel Industries Limited in Jordan. The article lists pay, contract terms, which costs the employer bears and which the worker bears, the documents to bring, and the walk-in interview on 20 September 2024 at the Bangladesh-Korea Technical Training Centre in Mirpur, Dhaka.

facts.statement: Through Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL), Tasker Apparel Industries Limited (তাস্কার অ্যাপারেল ইন্ডাস্ট্রিজ লিমিটেড) of Jordan is recruiting 250 women garment workers from Bangladesh for the post of female machine operator.

For the BOESL Jordan (Tasker Apparel) female machine operator posts, candidates must have practical experience in the relevant work; no educational qualification applies. The article gives the age limit two ways: 20 to 35 years in the body text and 18 to 30 years in the job description list.
facts.source_in_article: BOESL notice (the two age ranges disagree within the article)

facts.statement: Workers returned from Jordan or other countries will get priority for the BOESL Jordan garment posts on the basis of qualification and skill in the relevant work.
Pay for the BOESL Jordan female machine operator post at Tasker Apparel is printed as 125 'Jordan dollar' (১২৫ জর্ডান ডলার); the job is contractual with a 3-year contract that is renewable.
Terms of the BOESL Jordan garment job: 8 hours duty a day, 6 days a week, with overtime available; other conditions follow Jordan's labour law.

For the BOESL Jordan garment job the employer provides accommodation, food, primary medical treatment and transport costs; the article's introduction says accommodation, food and medical care are free.
The Jordanian employer pays the airfare to join the job and the airfare to return to Bangladesh after satisfactorily completing three years of service.

For selected workers in the BOESL Jordan recruitment, the employing company bears all costs for BOESL's service charge, departure (embarkation) tax, 15 percent VAT on the service charge, BOESL registration fee, smart card fee and Wage Earners' Welfare fee.
Selected workers in the BOESL Jordan recruitment must themselves pay the medical fee and the fingerprint fee (amounts not given).
Anyone with a case against her in Bangladesh or in Jordan is ineligible for the BOESL Jordan recruitment; a candidate with more than one passport must bring all of them.
Walk-in interview for the BOESL Jordan women garment worker recruitment: Friday 20 September 2024 at 8 am at the Bangladesh-Korea Technical Training Centre, Darus Salam Road, Mirpur, Dhaka.

To bring to the BOESL Jordan interview: CV; four passport-size colour photos with white background; original passport and four sets of colour photocopies of the passport's photo page; voter ID card or birth registration; current office ID card or attendance card; educational and experience certificates.

headline_en: Bangladesh embassy in Bahrain holds summer awareness programme for migrant workers
summary_en: A press-release style report: on Thursday 29 August 2024 the Bangladesh Embassy in Bahrain held a summer awareness event for Bangladeshi workers at a building under construction in the Seef area, with Bahrain's Labour Ministry, the Labour Market Regulatory Authority and IOM. Speakers stressed heat and site-safety rules, Bahrain's midday outdoor work ban in July and August, and the government hotline for reporting employers who force work during the ban.

facts.statement: By decision of Bahrain's Labour Ministry, working under direct sunlight and in open places was banned from 12 noon to 4 pm during July and August (the 2024 summer ban referred to at the event).
facts.source_in_article: Hussain Al-Hussaini, head of awareness and guidance, Bahrain Labour Ministry

facts.statement: If a sponsor or supervisor forces a worker to work during Bahrain's summer midday work ban, the worker can complain by calling the Bahrain government hotline 80008001; the ministry concerned will investigate and take the necessary steps.
facts.source_in_article: Hussain Al-Hussaini, head of awareness and guidance, Bahrain Labour Ministry

facts.statement: The Bahrain Labour Ministry official urged workers to follow all safety guidelines on site, including wearing a high-visibility jacket, helmet and safety shoes.

The Bangladesh Embassy's charge d'affaires in Bahrain told workers to follow all health and safety guidelines set by the Bahrain government, drink enough water and, for safety, not work in the fierce midday sun.
facts.source_in_article: Charge d'affaires A K M Mohiuddin Kayes, Bangladesh Embassy in Bahrain

facts.statement: At the embassy's summer awareness event for Bangladeshi construction workers in the Seef area of Bahrain, the embassy distributed thermos flasks, juice and lunch to all workers present and gave free medical coupons to all the Bangladeshi workers.

The event was chaired by charge d'affaires A K M Mohiuddin Kayes and conducted by embassy first secretary Md. Mahfuzur Rahman; taking part were Hussain Al-Hussaini of Bahrain's Labour Ministry, Rana Al-Ahmad, preventive inspection specialist of the Labour Market Regulatory Authority, and Fatima Mohammed of the International Organization for Migration.

headline_en: Action if money of workers who could not go to Malaysia is not refunded within 15 days: State Minister
summary_en: At a 4 July 2024 press conference, State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury said recruiting agencies must refund, by 18 July, the money of workers who paid but could not enter Malaysia before the 31 May 2024 deadline, or face legal action. The article gives the approval and departure numbers, the investigation committee timeline, and notes that the minister said nothing about the syndicate or overcharging allegations.

facts.statement: State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury said on 4 July 2024 that the money of workers who could not go to Malaysia must be refunded within 15 days, by 18 July 2024, otherwise legal action would be taken.

At a meeting on Wednesday 3 July 2024 with BAIRA, the association of recruiting agency owners, the agencies agreed to refund; an agency will refund exactly as much money as the worker can show proof of having deposited.

100 private Bangladeshi agencies were approved to send workers to Malaysia; any other agency wanting to send workers had to send through them. The papers of the workers who could not go are held, more or less, by all 100 agencies.

Asked about the liability of the 100 agencies for workers failing to reach Malaysia, the state minister said all were more or less responsible. He said many had sold land or cattle or taken loans to deposit the money.

The state minister hoped Malaysia's labour market would reopen soon: a meeting of the two countries' joint technical committee was due at the end of July 2024, after which he said the market would reopen.
Workers who could not go to Malaysia at the last moment are to be kept on a priority list so that they can go first when the labour market reopens.
31 May 2024 was the last date for workers to enter Malaysia; many could not reach the country by then for various reasons.

According to the 4 July 2024 press conference, 532,000 (5 lakh 32 thousand) workers were approved to go to Malaysia, 476,000 (4 lakh 76 thousand) finally went, and 17,000 workers who held clearance could not go.

The ministry formed an investigation committee on 2 June 2024 over the workers who could not go to Malaysia; the committee submitted its report on 24 June 2024. 2,055 workers lodged complaints with documents to the committee.

At the press conference the state minister spoke only about compensation for the stranded workers; he said nothing about the formation of a syndicate in the Malaysia market or about workers being charged several times the government-fixed amount, saying he would speak in detail later.

headline_en: Attempt to shut the Probashi Kalyan Desk at Shahjalal Airport's third terminal
summary_en: The Probashi Kalyan (Expatriates' Welfare) Desk, which serves migrant workers at Bangladesh's three international airports, was not being allocated space in the new third terminal of Dhaka's Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, expected to open for international flights in October 2024. The Civil Aviation Authority said clearance checks would be automated and welfare handled through the terminal's information centre; the Wage Earners' Welfare Board and the research body RMMRU argued the desk's help to departing, sick, deported and deceased migrants must continue.

facts.statement: All three of Bangladesh's international airports have a Probashi Kalyan Desk (Expatriates' Welfare Desk) to serve migrants when leaving and arriving; the desk verifies new workers' clearance, receives sick workers and receives the bodies of deceased migrants.
The Probashi Kalyan Desk works under the Wage Earners' Welfare Board, which is run from a fund made up of expatriates' own money.

Every worker going abroad must take clearance from BMET (Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training) and is given a smart card; at the airport the Probashi Kalyan Desk verifies this clearance so that no worker becomes a victim of human trafficking.

Workers on leave from the Middle East must carry their leave permission when they fly back; they print it out at the airport's Probashi Kalyan Desk, whose staff also check and help put all their papers in order.
The Probashi Kalyan Desk assists migrants who return physically or mentally ill and those who return on an outpass (travel permit) after being detained by police abroad.
When migrants' bodies arrive from abroad, the airport Probashi Kalyan Desk receives the body, hands it over to the family and pays the grant for burial.

On average more than 3,000 new workers go abroad from Bangladesh every day according to Wage Earners' Welfare Board officials; the board's director Shoaib Ahmad Khan put it at three to four thousand new workers a day, besides returning old workers.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board officials; director (additional secretary) Shoaib Ahmad Khan

facts.statement: The Probashi Kalyan Desk was not being allocated space in the third terminal of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka; on 24 June 2024 the desk wrote to the BMET director general asking for urgent steps to secure its place, with copies to the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry and the Wage Earners' Welfare Board.
The desk's letter said international flight operations at the newly built third terminal of Dhaka airport could begin in October 2024.

At a 10 June 2024 meeting of all airport agencies, the Civil Aviation Authority (CAAB) chairman said the present way of checking BMET emigration clearance would not exist in the third terminal: everything would be verified online in an automated system, with the immigration department's database integrated with BMET's database.
facts.source_in_article: CAAB chairman, as reported in the desk's letter

facts.statement: The airport's executive director told the 10 June 2024 meeting that any welfare activity for migrants in the third terminal would be run through the terminal's information centre.
facts.source_in_article: airport executive director, as reported in the desk's letter

facts.statement: Wage Earners' Welfare Board officials said that if clearance verification passes to the police immigration department, the desk's opportunity to verify clearance (to prevent trafficking) will end, and migrants will suffer if the desk is closed, since most migrant workers have little or no education and need help at the airport.

CAAB member (operations and planning) Air Commodore A F M Atiquzzaman said the services the Probashi Kalyan Desk provides are planned within the third terminal's operating structure; the terminal will be operated by a Japanese organisation, so a request for separate space must be made to that organisation.
facts.source_in_article: CAAB member Air Commodore A F M Atiquzzaman

headline_en: Two young men from Sunamganj die in the Mediterranean before reaching Italy
summary_en: Two young men from Sunamganj, Shahibur Rahman alias Manna (22) and Rezaul Islam (24), died on a boat from Libya to Italy that left on 21 June 2024; fellow passengers who reached Italy told relatives by phone that the two fell ill and died on the way. Shahibur's family had paid a Brahmanbaria broker BDT 8.5 lakh plus a further 1 lakh and monthly expenses during his 10 months in Libya. Families were asking local officials to help bring the bodies home, whose location was unknown.

facts.statement: Shahibur Rahman alias Manna (22) of Toler Bon village, Shimulbak union, Shantiganj upazila, Sunamganj and Rezaul Islam (24) of Doulatpur village, Jawa Bazar union, Chhatak upazila, Sunamganj died in the Mediterranean on the same boat from Libya before reaching Italy; details of how and where were not yet known.
facts.source_in_article: relatives, citing other Sunamganj passengers on the boat

facts.statement: Other Sunamganj men on the same 'game' boat told Rezaul's brother by WhatsApp after reaching Italy that Rezaul and Shahibur had fallen ill and died on the way; the survivors were placed in various camps in Italy and did not know where the two bodies were kept.
facts.source_in_article: cousin Imran Ahmad, citing Rezaul's brother Nazrul Islam

facts.statement: Shahibur Rahman's family agreed BDT 8.5 lakh with a broker named Ujjal Ahmad of Brahmanbaria, contacted through one or two villagers who had reached Italy the same way; with that payment Shahibur went to Libya 10 months before June 2024.

While Shahibur waited in Libya for the 'game' (the final sea crossing), his family sent expense money every month; the broker then said he would not be put on the 'game' unless another BDT 1 lakh was paid, which the family borrowed at interest and sent.
Shahibur Rahman was put on the 'game' boat from Libya towards Italy on Friday 21 June 2024, after about 10 months in Libya; he spoke to his family for the last time a day before.
Rezaul Islam left about a year before June 2024, going first to Dubai, then via Egypt to Libya; on 21 June 2024 he phoned to say he was boarding the 'game' from Libya to Italy.
Rezaul Islam's elder brother Nazrul Islam, who is in Oman (two elder brothers work there), phoned the family on the evening of Wednesday 26 June 2024 with the news of his death.

To seek help bringing the body back, Rezaul Islam's cousin Imran Ahmad took a certificate from the union parishad chairman and informed the Chhatak upazila nirbahi officer (UNO) on 27 June 2024; UNO Golam Mustafa said he had received the family's application and would give the necessary cooperation.
facts.source_in_article: cousin Imran Ahmad; Chhatak UNO Golam Mustafa

facts.statement: Shimulbak union parishad chairman Md. Shahinur Rahman said Shahibur's family had informed him and he would talk to the upazila administration and take the initiative on how the body could be brought home.
facts.source_in_article: Shimulbak UP chairman Md. Shahinur Rahman

headline_en: 'Our happiness never came home'
summary_en: Ali Hawladar (35), a battery-rickshaw driver from Shibchar, Madaripur, died when a migrant boat that left Libya on Monday 17 June 2024 sank near Italy's southern coast; at least 11 died and more than 60, including children, went missing. He had gone to Libya via Dubai two months earlier under a BDT 16 lakh contract with a local broker. Local officials and police said they had no official confirmation or list yet but would help the family, including with bringing the body back.

facts.statement: A migrant boat that left the Libyan coast on Monday 17 June 2024 with about 70 migrants sank near the southern coast of Italy; at least 11 migrants died and more than 60, including children, went missing.
According to local sources, three men from Shibchar, Madaripur, including Ali Hawladar and Sabbir Hossain, were among those killed in the 17 June 2024 boat sinking off southern Italy.

Ali Hawladar (35) of Khankandi, Shibchar, Madaripur went to Libya via Dubai two months before June 2024 through a local Madaripur broker under a contract of BDT 16 lakh; his in-laws' family provided the money.
facts.source_in_article: police and relatives; uncle-in-law Abdus Salam Ukil

facts.statement: Ali Hawladar's route was Bangladesh to Dubai to Libya, then an engine boat from the Libyan coast towards Italy on Monday 17 June 2024; he had told his wife by phone the day before Eid that their 'game' (Mediterranean boat crossing) would be on Eid day.

Ali Hawladar's family confirmed his death on the night of Tuesday 18 June 2024; he left a wife, a six-year-old son and a one-year-old daughter. His father Yunus Hawladar said he had not agreed to the journey.

Shibchar UNO Abdullah Al Mamun said the administration had not yet been able to confirm the death; if the family asks for help, the administration will give overall assistance including bringing the body back.

Madaripur Superintendent of Police Masud Alam said police had heard three Madaripur youths died in the sinking but had received no list from IOM or from the state; police were inquiring about the accused brokers and would give the family all legal assistance.

headline_en: Malaysia is not extending the time for taking workers: High Commissioner
summary_en: After meeting State Minister Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury on 5 June 2024, Malaysia's High Commissioner in Dhaka Haznah Md. Hashim said Malaysia was not extending the 31 May deadline for worker entry, which applied equally to all 15 source countries. She rejected, for lack of evidence, BAIRA's claim that Malaysia issued e-visas on 2 June after the deadline. The state minister said an investigation committee would examine why workers could not go and that those with a BMET card or e-visa would be compensated.

facts.source_in_article: Malaysian High Commissioner Haznah Md. Hashim

facts.statement: The High Commissioner said Malaysia takes workers from 15 countries and the same deadline was set for all; nothing separate was done for Bangladesh and Malaysia wants to keep the same policy for all countries.

headline_en: 'My boy's dream came back as a corpse'
summary_en: The bodies of eight Bangladeshis who died in February 2024 on a boat from Libya to Italy, in the Mediterranean off Tunisia, reached Dhaka on 2 May 2024 on a Saudia flight and were sent to Dhaka Medical College morgue for a second autopsy before handover. Relatives said brokers packed 52 people on a boat for 30, forced the eight below deck and beat them when they tried to come up, so they died of torture and lack of oxygen. Families accuse two Muksudpur brokers of taking BDT 10 to 15 lakh from each.

facts.statement: Eight Bangladeshis died on a boat in the Mediterranean off Tunisia, on the way from Libya to Italy, from torture by brokers according to relatives; five were from Rajoir, Madaripur and three from Muksudpur, Gopalganj. A Pakistani national also died and the local coast guard rescued several alive.

The eight dead were: Sajib Kazi (19), son of Mizanur Rahman Kazi, Kodalia village, Rajoir; Mamun Sheikh (22), son of Yusuf Ali Sheikh, Paschim Swarmangal village; Sajal Bairagi (22), son of Sunil Bairagi, Sendiar village; Nayan Biswas (24), son of Paritosh Biswas, Uttarpara village (elsewhere the article says Kadambari); Kawsar (22), Keshardia village; and from Muksudpur, Gopalganj: Rifad (21), son of Dadan Mia, Bardia village; Md. Rasel (20), Fateypatti area; and Isrul Kayes Apon (22), son of Pannu Sheikh, Goylakandi village.

The group left home in Rajoir (Madaripur) and Muksudpur (Gopalganj) for Italy on 14 January 2024, flew via Dubai to Libya, and on 14 February 2024 set off from Libya for Italy in an engine boat arranged by brokers.

Relatives said the brokers took 52 people on a small boat that could carry 30; the eight who died were forced to stay under the deck, tried to come out because of lack of oxygen, and were beaten by the brokers and sent back down, dying from the torture and oxygen shortage.
facts.source_in_article: relatives of the dead, speaking at Dhaka airport on 2 May 2024

facts.statement: Relatives allege that Rahim Sheikh of Gazaria village and Mosharraf Kazi of Sundardi village, both in Muksudpur, Gopalganj and active members of a trafficking ring, lured the men and took BDT 10 to 15 lakh from each.

The eight bodies arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka on a Saudia Airlines flight at 12:20 pm on Thursday 2 May 2024; a victim's father noted his son died in February and the body arrived in May. The Rajoir police officer-in-charge said the bodies were brought home by the government.
facts.source_in_article: relatives; Rajoir OC Md. Asaduzzaman Hawladar

facts.statement: Instead of being handed to the waiting families at the airport, the eight bodies were sent to the Dhaka Medical College Hospital morgue for autopsy, with handover to families planned after the autopsy on Friday 3 May 2024; a brother complained an autopsy had already been done in Tunisia.

The members of the broker ring had been in hiding since the incident; Rajoir OC Md. Asaduzzaman Hawladar said legal help would be given if the families sought it and legal action would be taken against the brokers on the families' complaint.
facts.source_in_article: relatives; Rajoir OC Md. Asaduzzaman Hawladar

headline_en: 'The broker said he'll return my son, I am waiting on him'
summary_en: Nine people, eight of them Bangladeshis from Rajoir (Madaripur) and Muksudpur (Gopalganj), died when a boat carrying migrants from Libya towards Italy sank in the Mediterranean off Tunisia in mid-February 2024; families got confirmation through the embassy in Libya on 20 February 2024. The article names the dead, traces the Dubai-Libya-'game house' route, records what families paid (BDT 10 to 15 lakh each) and names two accused brokers who have fled.

facts.statement: Nine people died when a boat carrying migrants illegally by sea from Libya to Italy sank in the Mediterranean off the Tunisian coast; eight were Bangladeshis (five from Rajoir upazila, Madaripur and three from Muksudpur, Gopalganj) and one was reported to be a Pakistani national. The local coast guard rescued several alive.
Families were confirmed of the young men's deaths on the morning of Tuesday 20 February 2024 through the embassy in Libya.

The Bangladeshi dead were named as Sajib Kazi (19), son of Mizanur Rahman Kazi, Kodalia village, Rajoir; Mamun Sheikh (22), son of Yusuf Ali Sheikh, Paschim Swarmangal village; Sajal Bairagi (22), son of Sunil Bairagi, Sendiar village; Nayan Biswas (24), son of Paritosh Biswas, Uttarpara village; Kawsar (22), Keshardia village; Rifad (21), son of Dadan Mia, Bardia village, Muksudpur; Md. Rasel (20), Fateypatti area; and Isrul Kayes Apon (22), son of Pannu Sheikh, Goylakandi village.

Several young men from Rajoir and Muksudpur left home for Italy on 14 January 2024; they were first taken to Dubai, kept there a few days, then taken to Libya, where the broker put them in a 'game house'; from that house an engine boat left the Libyan coast for Italy on Wednesday (about 14 February 2024).
According to relatives and local sources in this report, when the boat entered the Mediterranean off Tunisia its engine developed a fault, the boat caught fire and then sank.

Pannu Sheikh of Goylakandi village, Gopalganj said he paid BDT 11 lakh for his son Isrul Kayes Apon through a distant relative by marriage (beai); he said the broker had told him he would return his son and he was waiting on that.

Farmer Paritosh Biswas of Uttarpara village, Kadambari union, Rajoir said he borrowed and collected BDT 10 lakh to send his son Nayan Biswas abroad, and knew something was wrong when there was no contact for four or five days.
Mizanur Rahman Kazi said he borrowed and sold land to send his son Sajib Kazi; the son's last words by phone were that the 'game' was about to happen and he would call on reaching Italy.

Relatives allege that Rahim Sheikh of Gazaria village, Muksudpur, and Mosharraf Kazi, son of Badsha Kazi of Sundardi village, Raghdi union, Muksudpur, active members of a human trafficking ring, lured the men and took BDT 10 to 15 lakh from each.
A cousin of victim Sajib Kazi said the brokers' words were sweet before they took the money, but after taking it their actions did not match their words; the family intends to seek legal help.
All members of the accused broker ring were absconding after the accident and their mobile phones were switched off when called repeatedly.

Madaripur Superintendent of Police Masud Alam said broker rings are active in various areas of Madaripur and Gopalganj and legal action against them is ongoing; if the victims' families file a written complaint, a case will be taken and strict action taken against the brokers. He said ordinary people must also be aware or such deaths will not decrease.
Paritosh Biswas asked the government to arrange for his son's body to be brought home quickly.

headline_en: 7,500 prisoners in Saudi jails; government wants copy of verdict on the two executions
summary_en: Receiving the body of Md. Shahed Ahmed, a Bangladeshi worker killed in the 10 October 2026 Houthi attack on Riyadh's King Khaled International Airport, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said on 23 October 2026 that about 7,500 Bangladeshis are in Saudi prisons and that Bangladesh has formally asked Saudi Arabia for the verdict on two Bangladeshis who were executed. She gave figures on Bangladeshis killed in the Middle East conflict, said talks are under way on visas of workers stuck in Bangladesh, and described where workers abroad lodge complaints.

facts.statement: About 7,500 (seven and a half thousand) Bangladeshis are held in prisons in various cities of Saudi Arabia, according to State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam

facts.statement: After two Bangladeshis were executed in Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh summoned the Saudi ambassador and formally wrote to the Saudi government asking for a copy of the verdict; as of 23 October 2026 detailed information about the two had not been received.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam

facts.statement: The Saudi government from time to time sends Bangladesh lists of people convicted of various offences and held in prison; the government was checking whether the two executed Bangladeshis' names were on those lists.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam

facts.statement: When information is received that a Bangladeshi has been convicted abroad, Bangladesh contacts that country's government through diplomatic channels and also discusses whether there is scope for remission of the sentence; the Foreign Ministry works on such cases together with the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry and, on legal matters, the Home Ministry and others.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam

facts.statement: Bangladeshi worker Md. Shahed Ahmed of Madla village, Shajahanpur upazila, Bogura was killed in an attack by the armed group Houthi on King Khaled International Airport, Riyadh on 10 October 2026. He worked as a plumber on the Jeddah project of a Saudi contracting firm, held a work permit (iqama) in Saudi Arabia, and was returning via Riyadh to Jeddah after leave at home following his brother's death.

Two Bangladeshis were killed in the 10 October 2026 attack on Riyadh airport: Shahed Ahmed and Md. Nasrullah Badarpuri of Badarpur village, Nangalkot upazila, Cumilla; the Foreign Ministry said at the time that 24 more Bangladeshis were injured.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign Ministry (as stated at the time)

facts.statement: Shahed Ahmed's body reached Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka after 8 am on Friday 23 October 2026; the body and assistance from the government were handed to his wife Kohinur Akter Kakoli, with the state minister present.
More than 40 lakh (4 million) Bangladeshis work in Saudi Arabia, the state minister said, which is why Bangladeshi workers risk being casualties if there is war or any accident there.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam

facts.statement: In the six months to 23 October 2026, the bodies of 11 Bangladeshis killed because of conflict in the Middle East were brought home; Shahed Ahmed was the 11th.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam

facts.statement: In the month to 23 October 2026 three Bangladeshis were killed in missile attacks in Saudi Arabia; one body arrived on 23 October and efforts were under way to bring the others home quickly.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam

facts.statement: Talks are under way with Saudi Arabia on extending the visa validity and renewing the visas of migrant workers stuck in Bangladesh because of the Middle East conflict.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam

facts.statement: Every Bangladesh mission abroad has a labour welfare wing, staffed by officers of the Expatriates' Welfare or Labour ministries, where migrant workers usually lodge their complaints.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam

facts.statement: Responding to complaints that migrants do not get proper help from embassies and missions, the state minister said helping migrants is the duty of missions and government, and that any negligence by a mission will be looked into and action taken.
facts.source_in_article: State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam

headline_en: Old and unrelated videos being spread about the execution of two Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia
summary_en: A fact-check published 20 October 2026: videos and photo cards circulating after the 14 October 2026 execution of two Bangladeshis, Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akter, in Saudi Arabia are a 2015 execution video of a Myanmar woman and footage of another migrant's coffin; the bodies have not come home and the claim that the two were a married couple on Umrah is unsupported. The article also reports Bangladesh's diplomatic notes to Saudi Arabia, the Saudi account of the trial, and Nazrul's family's account of his migration, arrest and their costs.

facts.statement: On 14 October 2026 the Saudi Press Agency (SPA), citing Saudi Arabia's Interior Ministry, reported that the death sentences of two Bangladeshi nationals, Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akter, had been carried out.
facts.source_in_article: Saudi Press Agency citing the Saudi Interior Ministry

facts.statement: On 15 October 2026 the Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah sent a diplomatic note to the Saudi Foreign Ministry asking for details about the two executed Bangladeshis; on 18 October the note was given again to the Saudi ambassador in Dhaka. A person named Sakhawat Hossain (designation not given in the article) confirmed the meeting and the further note but declined to give details.

Foreign Ministry officials said that in the Jeddah discussion Bangladesh's consul general asked why the information about the punishment had been left out although both names were on the prisoner lists Saudi Arabia sends regularly.

Bangladesh's new diplomatic note asks for the full details of the case against the two executed Bangladeshis, the steps taken during the judicial process, and whether they had any opportunity at all to defend themselves after being convicted.

The Saudi side told the meeting that after the two were arrested in August 2023, a lower court first sentenced them following due judicial process, then a panel of 13 judges at the appeal court upheld the death sentences, and the sentences were carried out in separate cells designated for women and men.
facts.source_in_article: Saudi side, as reported by Dhaka officials

facts.statement: The beheading video circulating as the execution of the two Bangladeshis is an old 2015 video of the execution of Laila bint Abdul Muttalib Basim, a Myanmar national living in Saudi Arabia, convicted of torturing, sexually abusing and killing her husband's six-year-old daughter; reverse image search finds January 2015 reports by Middle East Eye, Daily Mail, Times of Israel and Dawn.

As of 11:20 am on Tuesday 20 October 2026 the bodies of the two executed Bangladeshis had not returned to Bangladesh: Shariful Islam, deputy director (welfare) and office head of the Probashi Kalyan Desk at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, said 'the bodies have not come yet'. The viral coffin video is of another Saudi-based migrant's body.
facts.source_in_article: Shariful Islam, Probashi Kalyan Desk, Dhaka airport

facts.statement: Social media claims that the two executed Bangladeshis were husband and wife who went to Saudi Arabia for Umrah instead of a honeymoon were not supported by any media report; Nazrul's father Abdul Basir said Nazrul was unmarried and the family knows nothing about the woman executed with him.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo verification; father Abdul Basir

facts.statement: According to his family, Nazrul Islam went to Saudi Arabia on 10 November 2022 and worked as a cleaner at the Haram Sharif in Mecca; Saudi police arrested him eight months after his arrival and he remained in Saudi prison from then on.

Nazrul's family learned of his detention a month after the arrest; from prison he could occasionally speak to his parents for a few minutes (his mother said he called about once a month for one to two minutes); the last call was on 11 October 2026 and lasted two to two and a half minutes.
Nazrul's family was told of his execution by a phone call from someone in Saudi Arabia at about 7:30 pm Bangladesh time on Wednesday 14 October 2026.

Nazrul Islam's father Abdul Basir said he borrowed BDT 6 lakh from relatives to send his son to Saudi Arabia; in the first seven to eight months the son sent home about BDT 1.5 lakh, and then spent three years in prison.
Nazrul's father demanded that the government bring his son's body home quickly; his mother said the charge against her son was false and she wants to see his body one last time.
facts.source_in_article: father Abdul Basir; mother Rahima Begum

facts.statement: A photo circulated as the two executed Bangladeshis' coffins is from a 9 May 2026 report: the body of Murad Sheikh of Goalanda upazila, Rajbari, killed in a road accident in Saudi Arabia, reached Bangladesh 16 days after his death and was taken from Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport to his village on the morning of 9 May 2026 and buried after an 11 am funeral.
facts.source_in_article: 9 May 2026 news report found by reverse image search

facts.statement: Related-story headlines embedded in the article say Dhaka questioned why the punishment was left unstated when the two names were on the prisoner list, and call the two executions a final warning bell.
facts.source_in_article: related-story headlines embedded in the article

headline_en: The government itself must make clear it is not involved in the Malaysia syndicate: Jamaat Ameer
summary_en: At a Jamaat-e-Islami seminar at the National Press Club on 17 September 2026, opposition leader and Jamaat Ameer Shafiqur Rahman said 25 agencies had been finalised to send workers to Malaysia and demanded the government explain the selection criteria, citing media reports that some have no prior experience and hearsay that BDT 15 to 22 crore is being invested. He alleged an old syndicate built by a man called Dato Sri Amin is still operating and warned against the Malaysia market closing a fourth time.

facts.statement: Opposition leader and Jamaat-e-Islami Ameer Shafiqur Rahman said on 17 September 2026 that 25 agencies had been finalised for sending workers to Malaysia; he said it appeared they would be 'master agencies' with associate agencies under them.
Shafiqur Rahman demanded the government make clear on what criteria the 25 agencies were selected, saying media had already reported that some of them have no previous experience.
facts.source_in_article: Jamaat Ameer Shafiqur Rahman, citing media reports

facts.statement: Shafiqur Rahman said 'we are hearing' that BDT 15 to 22 crore is being invested there (to become one of the selected Malaysia agencies) and that if so it could not happen without involvement of the government, which must itself make clear that it is not involved.
facts.source_in_article: Jamaat Ameer Shafiqur Rahman (hearsay, as he put it)

facts.statement: Shafiqur Rahman said Malaysia's labour market has been closed three times and that he does not want it to close a fourth time after reopening; he demanded a transparent sending process with no opening for any syndicate and an end to exploitation of Bangladeshi workers through the syndicate.

Shafiqur Rahman alleged that a person named Dato Sri Amin built a syndicate in the Malaysia labour market during the 'fascist government's' time, that it is still operating, and that some leaders still hold secret meetings with him.

Shafiqur Rahman called on Bangladesh to negotiate with Malaysia over the labour market the way Nepal, Sri Lanka, Pakistan and Indonesia do, and said the opposition would cooperate fully if the government took the initiative.
The opposition leader alleged that excluding expatriates' votes from local government elections is being considered, and said their voting must be ensured wherever they are.

The seminar, titled 'Syndicate and the Malaysian labour market: Bangladesh's partnership', was held at the Abdus Salam Hall of the National Press Club, Dhaka and organised by Jamaat-e-Islami; the keynote was presented by lawyer Shahriar Kabir and speakers included former BAIRA joint secretary general Mohammad Fakhrul Islam and former diplomat Sakib Ali.

headline_en: 79 migrants including Bangladeshis rescued near Greece's Crete island
summary_en: Greece's coast guard rescued 79 migrants, including Bangladeshi and Sudanese nationals, from two boats spotted by an EU drone near Kali Limenes port in southern Crete on Tuesday 25 August 2026. The report notes that Crete and nearby Gavdos have become the main entry route for asylum seekers into Greece, that arrivals have fallen about 31 percent year on year, and that Greece is pursuing a hard line including talks on 'return hubs' outside the EU.

facts.statement: Greece's coast guard rescued 79 migrants, including Bangladeshis and nationals of Sudan, near the island of Crete on Tuesday 25 August 2026; at least two women and two children were among them. The ANA news agency first reported 85 rescued, later confirmed as 79.
facts.source_in_article: Greek coast guard spokesperson; ANA news agency

facts.statement: The migrants were in two boats spotted by a European Union drone near the port of Kali Limenes in southern Crete; the coast guard had rescued hundreds of people from this sea area in recent days.
Crete and the nearby island of Gavdos have become the main entry route for asylum seekers into Greece; the islands lie about 320 kilometres (200 miles) from the Libyan coast.
Citing Greek Migration Ministry statistics, ANA said about 61,000 migrants arrived in Greece in the year to August 2025 and 42,000 in the following 12 months, a fall of about 31 percent.
facts.source_in_article: ANA news agency citing the Greek Migration Ministry

facts.statement: European authorities have tightened migration laws in recent years; the EU is working with transit countries, including Libya, to reduce irregular migration, and Greece's migration minister Thanos Plevris has adopted a strict policy on migrant entry.

Greece is considering a new initiative for screening migrants' applications and is in talks with Germany and several other EU countries about setting up return hubs (repatriation centres) outside the European Union.

headline_en: Remittances are counted; where is the account of migrants' suffering?
summary_en: An opinion column by Dr Selim Reza of North South University's Centre for Migration Studies arguing that Bangladesh counts remittances but not the social cost of migration: long family separation, children growing up without fathers, unlimited family expectations, property disputes over land bought with remittances, and unaddressed mental stress. It cites remittance and migrant-death statistics and recommends adding financial planning, family communication and mental wellbeing to pre-departure training, plus faster property dispute resolution, legal aid and mental health services.

facts.statement: About one crore (10 million) Bangladeshi citizens live and work in various countries, making Bangladesh the world's sixth largest origin country of international migrants.
facts.source_in_article: IOM, 2025, cited by columnist Dr Selim Reza

facts.statement: According to Bangladesh Bank, migrants sent USD 35.56 billion in remittances to Bangladesh through legal channels in fiscal year 2025-26, the highest in the country's history and 17.3 percent more than the previous fiscal year.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank, cited by the columnist

facts.statement: By the World Bank's reckoning Bangladesh is currently the world's eighth largest remittance-receiving country.
facts.source_in_article: World Bank, cited by the columnist

facts.statement: According to the Wage Earners' Welfare Board, the bodies of 4,813 Bangladeshi migrant workers were returned from abroad in 2024, the highest number so far.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board, cited by the columnist

facts.statement: Between 2015 and 2024 the bodies of about 38,000 Bangladeshi migrant workers came home; most were working-age people under 40.
facts.source_in_article: Wage Earners' Welfare Board, cited by the columnist

facts.statement: The columnist, drawing on interviews with Bangladeshi migrants for a recent social research study, reports that many migrant workers stay away from family for 5, 7 or even 10 years and many cannot come home on leave even once a year.

The column describes migrant workers' living conditions: most live on limited income, many are crowded into small rooms, work long hours in harsh weather and cut their own needs (medical care, nutritious food, rest) to send more money home; job loss, delayed wages and illness abroad are part of their reality.

The column warns that property bought with remittances (land, houses) is vulnerable because the owner is abroad: land grabbing, forged documents, boundary and inheritance disputes and court cases arise, often with close relatives (a brother, uncle or cousin), and running a court case from abroad is very difficult.

Various studies by the International Labour Organization and the International Organization for Migration have found that rates of anxiety, chronic stress and social isolation are significantly higher among migrant workers than in the general population.
facts.source_in_article: ILO and IOM studies, cited by the columnist

facts.statement: The columnist recommends that pre-departure training for outgoing workers include financial planning, family communication and mental wellbeing alongside language and job skills; community-based awareness programmes for families at home on financial awareness, marital relations, child-rearing and sharing responsibility; and faster settlement of property disputes, accessible legal aid, digital services and stronger mental health services.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Dr Selim Reza, Centre for Migration Studies, North South University

headline_en: Opposition demands a task force to solve expatriates' problems; ruling party also positive
summary_en: In a parliamentary discussion on 10 June 2026 under Rule 147, opposition leader Shafiqur Rahman proposed a parliamentary task force of MPs and experts to identify and solve expatriates' problems; the ruling party responded positively and suggested alternatives such as quickly forming the standing committee and an inter-ministry working committee. Specific problems raised include e-passports being refused over mismatches between MRP and NID data, slow repatriation of bodies, embassy attitudes, and the closed Malaysian labour market.

facts.statement: On Wednesday 10 June 2026 the opposition in the 13th Jatiya Sangsad, through a general motion under Rule 147 moved by opposition leader Shafiqur Rahman, demanded a parliamentary task force of MPs and experts to identify and solve expatriates' problems; the ruling party said such a task force could be formed. The motion sought only discussion and was not put to a vote.
facts.source_in_article: parliament proceedings; Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad

facts.statement: Shafiqur Rahman said the task force could travel to the countries where Bangladeshi workers have the most problems and hear from migrant workers and embassy officials.

Opposition leader Shafiqur Rahman told parliament that many expatriates applying for an e-passport face problems because the data in their MRP (machine readable passport) and national ID card do not match; small differences in vowel signs or spelling of a name, or a mismatch in age, mean many cannot get an e-passport, so many migrants are becoming undocumented abroad or risk becoming so.

Shafiqur Rahman demanded arrangements for bringing home quickly the bodies of people who die abroad, and called for an environment to bring back Bangladeshi researchers, scientists and technologists living abroad ('intellectual remittance').

Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said an alternative would be to quickly form the parliamentary standing committee on the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry and settle many issues there, and that a working committee of the Home, Foreign, Expatriates' Welfare and Civil Aviation ministries could be formed so that expatriates get proper respect and priority at airports and everywhere.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said the Prime Minister's first visit has been fixed for Malaysia, giving it importance precisely in order to open the Malaysian labour market.

State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare Nurul Haque said the Malaysian labour market opens once and closes again and is closed now; he said MPs want no syndicate there and the Prime Minister has given strict instructions that the government must not be given a bad name.

facts.statement: State Minister Nurul Haque said the kind of 'approach' needed at embassies is in many cases not happening.

headline_en: Broker hid the news of Mohibur's death for two days
summary_en: Mohibur Rahman (20) of Chhatak, Sunamganj died of starvation on a rubber boat that left Libya for Greece on 21 March 2026, lost its way and drifted for six days; 22 people on board died, most from Sunamganj, and the bodies were thrown into the sea. His broker Nabi Hossain, who is in Libya, told the family for two days that he had reached Greece and was in a camp; a survivor finally confirmed he was the first to die. His father had sold land and borrowed from moneylenders to pay BDT 13 lakh.

facts.statement: A rubber boat left Libya for Greece on 21 March 2026, lost its way in the Mediterranean and was at sea for six days; its fuel ran out and 22 people on board died one by one of starvation for lack of food and clean water, most of them from Sunamganj. The others were rescued off the Greek coast on Friday 27 March 2026, when the deaths became known.
The bodies of those who died on the Libya-Greece rubber boat stayed on board for two days; when they began to smell they were thrown into the sea on the broker's instruction.
News that 12 people from Sunamganj had died on the Libya-Greece boat reached their relatives in Bangladesh on the afternoon of Saturday 28 March 2026.

Broker Nabi Hossain concealed Mohibur Rahman's death for two days: when the family contacted him after the news of the deaths, he first said he would tell them later, then said Mohibur had reached Greece, was in a camp and could not talk now. The family learned on Monday 30 March 2026 that he was dead.

Suspicious, Mohibur's family went to the broker's home in Pagla; from there a relative, union parishad member Mohammad Sunu Mia, spoke to Nabi Hossain by phone, who confirmed Mohibur had been put on that boat but still avoided the question of his death. Survivor Maruf Ahmad of Sadipur village, Kolkolia union, Jagannathpur then phoned home to say Mohibur was the first on the boat to die and his body was set adrift with the others.
facts.source_in_article: relatives; UP member Mohammad Sunu Mia

facts.statement: Mohibur Rahman left home about four months before the end of March 2026 intending to reach Greece; he travelled via Saudi Arabia to Libya together with Maruf Ahmad, and at one point told his family he was suffering badly and begged to be brought home.
facts.source_in_article: cousin and UP member Mohammad Sunu Mia

facts.statement: To send his son to Greece, Mohibur's poor father Md. Nurul Amin sold land and borrowed at moneylenders' interest and paid BDT 13 lakh; the journey was arranged through Nabi Hossain of the Pagla area, Shantiganj upazila, Sunamganj, who is in Libya.
facts.source_in_article: cousin and UP member Mohammad Sunu Mia

facts.statement: Mohibur Rahman (20) was from Gaglajur village, Bhatgaon union, Chhatak upazila, Sunamganj, the eldest of three brothers and two sisters; he worked as a mason and his income supported the whole family.
A related-story headline embedded in the article reports the death by starvation of another young man from Sunamganj on the same Mediterranean boat.

headline_en: Remittances offer hope even amid the crisis
summary_en: A March 2026 banking report: despite unrest across the Middle East following the joint US-Israeli attack on Iran, remittances to Bangladesh rose sharply, with USD 1.92 billion arriving in the first 11 days of March 2026, up more than 44 percent year on year. Banks are paying more for remittance dollars (BDT 123.30), pushing up the import dollar rate, and economists advised Bangladesh Bank to hold on to reserves.

facts.statement: About 38 percent of Bangladesh's remittance income comes from the Gulf countries.

Since the joint United States and Israeli attack on Iran, there has been unrest across the Middle East and Bangladeshi migrants in Middle East countries are in difficulty and fear; even so, as of mid-March 2026 remittances to Bangladesh had taken no big hit and had in fact risen, though bank officials remain apprehensive.

According to Bangladesh Bank, USD 192 crore (1.92 billion) in remittances came to Bangladesh in the first 11 days of March 2026, including USD 18.30 crore on 11 March alone; in the same period of the previous year it was USD 133 crore, a rise of more than 44 percent.
From July to 11 March of fiscal year 2025-26, remittances to Bangladesh totalled USD 2,437.40 crore, against USD 1,982 crore in the same period of 2024-25, growth of about 23 percent.
On 11 March 2026 Bangladesh's foreign exchange reserves stood at USD 3,429 crore (34.29 billion); by the IMF's BPM-6 method they were USD 2,956 crore (29.57 billion, as printed).

Banks bought remittance dollars at BDT 123.30 on Thursday (about 12 March 2026), up from as much as BDT 122.90 on the Tuesday before; earlier remittance dollars could be bought at BDT 122. Because of war uncertainty, foreign remittance houses are asking a higher dollar price.
facts.source_in_article: officials of commercial banks dealing in dollars; bank sources

facts.statement: The dollar price for imports rose above BDT 123.50, from up to BDT 122.50 a week earlier; an importer said banks suddenly raised the import dollar rate by up to one taka.
Bangladesh Bank's published exchange-rate report showed the average dollar rate at BDT 122.33 on 3 March 2026, BDT 122.58 on Tuesday and BDT 122.75 on Thursday (about 12 March).
A top official of a private bank said Bangladesh Bank had signalled the dollar would not rise above BDT 123, but that this could not be held.

Syed Mahbubur Rahman, managing director of Mutual Trust Bank and former chairman of the Association of Bankers Bangladesh, said Bangladeshis in Middle East countries are frightened by the unrest but are still sending money home ahead of Eid, and many are sending money for zakat, which is why remittances rose.
facts.source_in_article: Syed Mahbubur Rahman, Mutual Trust Bank

facts.statement: Former Bangladesh Bank chief economist Mustafa K Mujeri said the government must stand by workers in Middle East countries and give any support they need there; he said several Middle East countries were damaged by the war and reconstruction after it ends will need extra workers, an opportunity Bangladesh can use.
facts.source_in_article: Mustafa K Mujeri, former chief economist, Bangladesh Bank

facts.statement: Eight leading economists, at a recent meeting with Bangladesh Bank, advised it to hold on to reserves to absorb the coming shock from the Middle East crisis, not to cut the policy interest rate yet, to arrange alternative energy sources to the Middle East and not to pass higher world prices on to consumers immediately.
facts.source_in_article: eight economists at a meeting with Bangladesh Bank

headline_en: 10 young men missing for 10 months on the illegal route to Italy
summary_en: Ten young men from Madaripur who left in January 2025 for Italy via Dubai and Libya have been missing since they boarded a boat from the Libyan coast in early April 2025. Families say local broker Peyara Begum and her ring promised direct passage to Italy for BDT 15 lakh, then the men were held and tortured in Libya for ransom of BDT 13 to 15 lakh each; families paid BDT 28 to 30 lakh in total. One family has filed a case and three people are under arrest; the broker's son denies the allegations.

facts.statement: Ten young men from Madaripur have been missing for about 10 months after setting out from the Libyan coast for Italy by engine boat at the start of April 2025; families do not know whether they are alive or dead.

The ten missing are: Limon Bepari (19), son of Anwar Bepari, Noyakandi, Kendua union, Madaripur Sadar; Rabiul Matubbar (22), son of Hemayet Matubbar, same area; Md. Joy Matubbar (20), son of Titu Matubbar, Dotterhat, Kendua union; Jidan Hossain Hawladar (18), son of Moktar Hawladar; Walid Hasan (19), son of Julhas Chokdar, Gachbaria, Mostafapur union; Mohammad Ali (22), Machkandi, Peyarpur union; Shariful Islam (27), son of Abul Bashar Matubbar, Machchar, Bajitpur union, Rajoir; Azmul Kha (30), son of Hashem Kha, Pakhulla; Tuhin Majumdar (23), son of Kalu Majumdar, Mollakandi; and Md. Mahabub Hossain (21), new bus stand area, Madaripur town.

The ten were lured with an offer to reach Italy for only BDT 15 lakh: the broker made a contract with each family to deliver the young man 'directly' to Italy for BDT 15 lakh. Instead they were taken to Dubai, then held in Libya for ransom.

The ten left home in January 2025; they were taken from Bangladesh first to Dubai, kept there a few days, then all were confined in a detention house in a city in Libya; in early April 2025 they set off through brokers by engine boat from the Libyan coast for Italy.

In Libya the broker ring physically and mentally tortured the ten Madaripur men for ransom and collected BDT 13 to 15 lakh in ransom from each family; in all, families say they gave the broker ring BDT 28 to 30 lakh each.

Anwar Bepari, father of missing Limon Bepari, said he handed over his son's passport and money to broker Peyara Begum and that a total of BDT 28 lakh was extracted, including while his son was held in Libya.

Titu Matubbar said his son Joy used to work at Peyara Begum's house, where he was lured; in Libya he was 'made to be caught by the mafia' once and was released after BDT 12 lakh was paid; there has been no news since April 2025.
Razia Begum, mother of missing Shariful Islam, said Peyara Begum and her people did not let her contact her son after 12 April 2025.

Peyara Begum, wife of Jahangir Dhali of Gazirchar, Kendua union, Madaripur Sadar, is named by families as the local broker who lured the ten; the reporter found that her elder son Fardin Dhali lives in Italy and directs the trafficking from there, her younger son Sourav Dhali collects money from migrants' families, and her brother Ali Akbar, plus Sabuj Kazi (son of Jalal Kazi) and Mujahid Sheikh (printed as 'Liakat Sheikh's Mujahid Sheikh'), who are brothers-in-law, are also involved.

Nobody was found at Peyara Begum's house; neighbours said she had been missing for about a month. Her son Sourav Dhali told Prothom Alo by phone that his mother lured no one, the men went voluntarily, and the family is being harassed with false allegations.

Madaripur Additional Superintendent of Police (crime and investigation) Mohammad Jahangir Alam said one of the ten missing men's families has filed a case and three people are under arrest in it; legal action will be taken if the other families file written complaints.

Madaripur police said they repeatedly tell people not to travel abroad through brokers, but no one listens, so many die early and families suffer financial loss; awareness is the only way to prevent trafficking.

headline_en: Give importance to the inclusion of migrant women
summary_en: Report of a roundtable on gender-sensitive, sustainable reintegration of returnee migrant women, held by UN Women and Prothom Alo in Dhaka on about 18 December 2025. A Wage Earners' Welfare Board official described the RAISE project for returnee workers (253,000 covered, about 7 percent women); NGO, ILO, BRAC, RMMRU and returnee-organisation speakers called for individual needs-based rehabilitation, airport-stage support, safety abroad and tackling stigma. Three returnee women from Jordan and Saudi Arabia said they had paid brokers and faced negative talk on return.

facts.statement: The RAISE project (Recovery and Advancement of Informal Sector Employment), implemented by the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry and the Wage Earners' Welfare Board, works on rehabilitation, skills development and employment of returnee migrant workers; under it 253,000 (2 lakh 53 thousand) returnee workers are being given registration, counselling and an incentive.
facts.source_in_article: A T M Mahbub-ul Karim, joint director, Wage Earners' Welfare Board

facts.statement: About 7 percent of the returnee workers covered by the RAISE project are women.
facts.source_in_article: A T M Mahbub-ul Karim, Wage Earners' Welfare Board

facts.statement: More than 4 lakh workers returned from abroad in 2020 and more returned up to 2025; it has not been possible to rehabilitate all returnees under the RAISE project (said in the context of extending the project).
facts.source_in_article: A T M Mahbub-ul Karim, Wage Earners' Welfare Board

facts.statement: Sumaiya Islam, executive director of Bangladesh Nari Sramik Kendra, said women workers do not need to pay money to go abroad, but this information has not reached the grassroots; she said women workers send home nearly all of their earnings.
facts.source_in_article: Sumaiya Islam, Bangladesh Nari Sramik Kendra

facts.statement: Three returnee women workers from Jordan and Saudi Arabia at the roundtable (Shahnaz Begum, Sathi Akter and Asma Begum) all said they had paid a broker to go abroad and all heard negative remarks in society after returning; they spent their money on things like children's medical treatment. Asma Begum now runs a tea stall in Dhaka.
facts.source_in_article: returnee workers Shahnaz Begum, Sathi Akter, Asma Begum

facts.statement: The government's Reintegration Policy for Returnee Migrant Workers 2024 includes the gender dimension.

ILO programme manager Rahnuma Salam Khan said a returning woman worker's rehabilitation begins at the airport, and that counselling, training and employment steps must each account for women's specific needs and be shared among ministries, NGOs and private organisations rather than one ministry.

BRAC associate director Shariful Hasan recommended ensuring every worker has a mobile phone in hand after going abroad, having embassies phone women workers to check on them, and writing a guideline on which agency does what at the airport when workers return; he also urged more initiatives for women to go to countries such as Hong Kong and Jordan for garment, caregiver and other work.

Shariful Hasan said the government should decide a woman's rehabilitation according to the circumstances in which she was forced to return, and that many good laws and policies exist but their implementation must be checked.

Other recommendations at the roundtable: person-by-person rehabilitation rather than just handing out a sewing machine or shop, with a strong referral mechanism (Shakirul Islam, Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program); government-led 'welfare centres' for returnees through public-private effort (Hasan Imam, Centre for Development Communication); and a system for returnees to fill in an information card at the airport, to be passed to the expatriates' welfare centre (Ananya Raihan, iSocial).

Syed Saiful Haque, chairperson of returnee workers' organisation WARBE, said the government has, though late, begun giving importance to rehabilitating returnee workers, and that returnee women are leading various associations.
Ananya Raihan of iSocial said financial support from donor agencies is decreasing, so a new economic model has to be built for this work.

headline_en: Illegal journey to Italy: broker reports death by 'boat sinking' in the Mediterranean
summary_en: Arman Mia (32) of Bhairab, Kishoreganj, a returnee from Malaysia, left on 7 November 2025 for Italy via Libya under a BDT 30 lakh deal with broker Jasim Uddin, who lives in Libya. The broker first told the family Arman had reached Italy, then that he was still preparing, and on 18 November phoned to say he had drowned the day before when a boat sank; the broker's mother heard he was shot. The family suspects he was tortured and killed and was preparing a written complaint to police.

facts.statement: Broker Jasim Uddin took from Arman Mia of Alukanda village, Bhairab, Kishoreganj a written transfer of seven decimals of land valued at BDT 20 lakh plus BDT 10 lakh in cash (a BDT 30 lakh deal) to deliver him to Italy by sea via Libya.

The broker promised to deliver Arman to Italy 'risk-free' in a special boat; after Arman reached Libya the broker told the family he had arrived in Italy, the next day sent a voice message saying he had not yet gone and preparations were under way, then became unreachable, and finally phoned to say Arman had died, telling the family not to make a fuss.
Arman Mia left Bangladesh on 7 November 2025 and reached Libya the same day (as the article states), intending to cross by sea to Italy.

On the morning of Tuesday 18 November 2025 broker Jasim Uddin phoned Arman Mia's family to say Arman died on Monday 17 November when a boat sank while crossing from Libya to Italy and that others on the boat also died; he could not say who they were or whether the body was recovered, and hung up.

The broker's mother Hamida Begum said her son told her of Arman's death too, but she heard there was gunfire at sea and Arman died of a gunshot. Arman's brother Nayan Mia said he does not believe the drowning story and suspects the broker ring tortured and killed him deliberately.
facts.source_in_article: Hamida Begum (broker's mother); brother Nayan Mia

facts.statement: Arman's family contacted acquaintances in Libya, who said they too had heard of his death but could not say how he died.

Jasim Uddin (45) of Fari Raghunathpur village, next to Alukanda in Bhairab, has been sending people abroad for several years and himself lives in Libya; he proposed the Italy trip to Arman by phone. headline_en: Learn the language and you can go to Japan on good pay, but Bangladesh is taking little of the opportunity
summary_en: An October 2025 economy feature on Japan's labour market for Bangladeshis: Japan's shrinking, ageing population means companies need foreign workers, and with Japanese language (a six to nine month course) Bangladeshis can earn roughly BDT 135,000 to 157,000 a month without paying brokers. It lists the open job sectors, wage basis, the 27 permitted recruiting agencies, yearly sending targets, and where Japanese can be learned (BMET technical training centres, private institutes, universities), while noting Bangladesh has only about 26,000 people in Japan against Nepal's 250,000 and a shortage of language teachers.

facts.statement: Pay and allowances for Bangladeshi workers in Japan are stated as BDT 135,000 to 157,000 a month (1 lakh 35 thousand to 1 lakh 57 thousand taka in Bangladeshi currency).

To go to Japan for work a person must know Japanese; the article says no job at all can be had in Japan without Japanese language training, that one can go after a six to nine month language course, and that there is later an opportunity to live there permanently.
The article says a person does not need to pay money and run after brokers to go to Japan.

Japan's birth rate fell in 2024 to its lowest in 125 years; its population fell to 12 crore 3 lakh (120.3 million) in October 2024, 9 lakh fewer than a year before; Japan's National Institute of Population and Social Security Research projects a 30 percent fall to 8 crore 70 lakh by 2070, when 4 in 10 people will be 65 or older. Japan announced a 3.6 trillion yen childcare policy package.
facts.source_in_article: reporter, citing the National Institute of Population and Social Security Research

facts.statement: Finance Adviser Salehuddin Ahmed, after visiting Japan from the third week of August to the first week of September 2025, said it is possible to send one lakh (100,000) workers from Bangladesh to Japan 'within three months' on condition that they know Japanese; he said the Japanese told him jobs are assured for Bangladeshis who know the language, and that the demand is not only for caregivers but other categories too.

Bangladesh was added in 2019 to the countries Japan takes workers from: the first memorandum of understanding with Japan was signed on 29 January 2019 and the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry issued a policy on it on 17 February 2019. Japan has long taken workers from China, Indonesia, Nepal, Myanmar, the Philippines, Mongolia, Thailand and Vietnam, among others.

According to Expatriates' Welfare Ministry sources, 26,000 Bangladeshis currently live in Japan; the Finance Adviser said Nepal has sent two and a half lakh (250,000) people to Japan, and that the Japanese told him Nepalis are very disciplined and recruiting agencies have no stranglehold there.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare Ministry sources; Finance Adviser Salehuddin Ahmed

facts.statement: The article says jobs are open in Japan in 14 sectors and lists: nursing care or caregiver, restaurant, construction, building cleaning, agriculture, food and beverage industry, service sector, materials processing, industrial packaging, electric and electronic equipment, shipbuilding, fisheries, car painting, welding and automobile mechanic or automotive parts manufacturing, and airport ground handling and aircraft maintenance (aviation).
For now Japan is taking most people as technical interns (TI) in caregiving, industrial packaging, and welding and automobile mechanics.
The Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry has formed a separate cell for those interested in going to Japan, called the 'Japan Cell'.

At a recent seminar Expatriates' Welfare Adviser Asif Nazrul said the cost of sending people to Japan is not very high, there is no scope to recruit people there with fake documents, and that he had asked Japan to give language training itself and take people, which Japan is interested in.

According to Expatriates' Welfare Ministry sources, Japan's largest current need for people from Bangladesh is in the nursing care category, 60,000 people; Japan's average life expectancy is 84 and about 70,000 people are aged 100 or more.

Ministry sources give the opportunity to send workers to Japan as 2,000 in 2026, 6,000 in 2027, 12,000 in 2028, 30,000 in 2029 and 50,000 in 2030; by sector, 40,000 could go in construction, 20,000 in factories, 20,000 as caregivers and 20,000 in agriculture and car servicing.

Under Japan's labour law a worker's minimum wage is stated as BDT 700 an hour in Bangladeshi currency; workers can work 8 hours a day, which the article works out to about BDT 135,000 a month; in some cases there is a limit of 44 working hours a week. Wages are paid into a bank account.

So far 27 recruiting agencies in Bangladesh have been permitted to give training and assist in sending people to Japan; the permission of one was cancelled over an allegation of taking money, and the rest are working.
facts.source_in_article: ministry source (speaker not clearly identified in the article)

facts.statement: It makes no difference whether Japanese is learned at a government or a private centre.
facts.source_in_article: ministry source (speaker not clearly identified in the article)

facts.statement: BMET (the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training, under the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry) has started Japanese language training through 32 centres; at some of its technical training centres (TTCs) a four-month Japanese language course has been introduced, with 40 trainees per course.

BMET training centres giving N4-level Japanese training are named as: Bangladesh-Korea TTC Mirpur, Mohila (Women's) TTC Mirpur, Bangladesh-Korea TTC Chattogram, Narsingdi TTC, Chapainawabganj TTC, Tangail TTC and Khulna TTC. N4 pass means having basic ability to understand Japanese; admission requires only an SSC pass certificate.

Further Japanese language centres opened under a 'hybrid model' are: Bangladesh-Korea TTC Mirpur, Mohila TTC Mirpur, Bangladesh-Korea TTC Chattogram, Chapainawabganj TTC, Khulna TTC, Moulvibazar TTC, Brahmanbaria TTC, Kishoreganj TTC, Kapasia TTC, Barishal TTC, Rajbari TTC and Chandpur Sadar TTC, among others.
After the language training workers sit an exam; those who pass get a further four months of training under Japanese management and are then taken to Japan as trainees (interns).

Private options for learning Japanese named in the article: the international language institute 'Ekush' in Mirpur (founder and CEO Nurul Islam Khan says many have gone to Japan after learning there); a residential training centre on 22 bighas at Birulia, Dhaka built by Kawai Group Japan Limited, where language and skills training by Japanese teachers started on 1 October (2025); and Dhaka University, Green University and North South University also teach Japanese.
facts.source_in_article: reporter; Nurul Islam Khan of Ekush

facts.statement: Ministry officials admit there is a shortage of skilled Japanese language teachers at the Japanese language training centres under BMET.

headline_en: 43,000 students can be sent to Japan in 3 years; government wants to use the opportunity
summary_en: At an 18 August 2025 seminar in Dhaka organised by Bdjobs and the Association of Japanese Language Institutes in Bangladesh (AJLIB), speakers said the interim government has decided to send 100,000 skilled workers to Japan and that with proper planning at least 43,000 students could be sent in three years. Bangladesh's ambassador in Japan said 22 organisations and more than 100 companies had hired Bangladeshi workers in the previous two months and stressed sending skilled people over sending quickly.

facts.statement: The interim government has recently decided to send one lakh (100,000) skilled workers to Japan, and a public-private joint initiative has been taken to build institutional capacity for learning Japanese.

The Chief Adviser's special envoy Lutfey Siddiqi said a Japan cell has been created on the Chief Adviser's instruction with special focus on Japan; the Japan Cell's focal person is named as Md. Hedayetul Islam Mondal.
