headline_en: Even after paying ransom, relatives cannot find 14 young men for five months
summary_en: Fourteen young men from Bajitpur union, Rajoir, Madaripur who left in February 2025 for Italy via Dubai (on visit visas) and Libya have not been heard from for five months. Families say broker Babul Hawladar took BDT 16 lakh each, then a further BDT 20 to 25 lakh each as ransom while the men were held in Libya, then fled with his family. Police say the families have shown little interest in filing cases and that 400 to 500 young men from the thana are still captive in Libya.

facts.statement: Fourteen young men aged 18 to 28 from Bajitpur union, Rajoir upazila, Madaripur, who set out illegally for Italy, have not been traceable for five months since reaching Libya via Dubai; they were to cross the Mediterranean by engine boat but have not been heard from since February 2025.

The fourteen missing are: Salman Bepari (son of Jahangir Bepari, Pakhulla village); Babul Shikdar (son of Moslem Shikdar, Chaurashi village); Sajjad Boyati (son of Mojibor Boyati); Badal Matubbar (son of Zakir Matubbar); Liton Roy (son of Kanai Roy); Bandhan Barai (son of Niranjan Barai); Emon Chowkidar (son of Alam Chowkidar, Kismaddi Bajitpur village); Nayan Matubbar (son of Ohidul Matubbar); Khalil Khalasi (son of Aziz Khalasi); Sohel Chowkidar (son of Sona Mia Chowkidar); Goutam Barai (son of Gouranga Barai, Noyakandi Bajitpur village); Imran Sardar (son of Samchu Sardar); Al Amin Boyati (son of Jalil Boyati, Srinathdi Bajitpur); and Ali Gharami (son of Siddiqur Rahman Gharami, Srinadi village).
The fourteen left home in February 2025 with the broker; they first went to Dubai on visit (tourist) visas, stayed a few days and then reached Libya.

Families allege that Babul Hawladar of the Bajitpur area, an active member of a trafficking ring, first took BDT 16 lakh from each family on the promise of Italy (collected while the men were held in a detention house in Libya), then showed them as captured by the Libyan 'mafia' and extracted a further BDT 20 to 25 lakh per person; relatives put the total at BDT 30 to 35 lakh per person.

Aziz Khalasi said broker Babul Hawladar took his son's passport by force promising to send him to Italy 'nicely'; after confining him in Libya he took BDT 16 lakh first, BDT 5 lakh four months later, and then, selling him to the mafia, another BDT 10 lakh; the son has neither been returned nor sent to Italy.

Niranjan Barai sold land and borrowed at interest to pay BDT 30 lakh for his son Bandhan Barai: first BDT 10 lakh on the claim he had been caught by the mafia, then BDT 5 lakh, then BDT 15 lakh; he says all the payments were recorded on video.

The pattern described: the broker gets the man to Libya, has him confined, collects the agreed contract money, then claims he has been seized by or sold to the 'mafia' and extracts repeated ransom payments; when relatives press him the broker stalls for a few days and then disappears.

Besides Babul Hawladar, victims say his daughters Sonia Akter and Shashi Akter and his wife Chunnu Begum are involved in the ring. His house in Bajitpur was found locked on about 23 July 2025; neighbours variously said he now lives in Dhaka with his family or has gone abroad; his phone was switched off.

Babul Hawladar's daughter Sonia Akter told Prothom Alo her father did not flee with anyone's money, that his job was only up to getting people to Libya, that he tried to help when relatives came after the men were caught by the mafia, and that neither he nor the family received any ransom money.
facts.source_in_article: Sonia Akter, daughter of the accused broker

facts.statement: Rajoir police officer-in-charge Masud Khan said the affected families were told to file cases but none showed much interest; police are keeping track of the brokers.
The Rajoir OC said 400 to 500 young men from the Rajoir thana area are still captive in Libya; some manage to reach Italy but many live in inhuman conditions in detention houses.

According to Madaripur district administration and police data, from 2019 to March 2023, 45 people from the district died on the way to Italy via Libya, at least 350 young men managed to return to Bangladesh from Libya after being tortured, and more than 300 are missing.

Runa Begum, wife of missing Sohel Chowkidar, said the family sold all its land and borrowed at interest to pay the broker lakhs of taka, has had no news of her husband for over five months, and is now going without food.
A related-story headline embedded in the article says a human trafficking case was filed over three missing young men and a father and son were arrested in Faridpur.

headline_en: The process of sending manpower abroad is made complex and long in order to commit corruption: Asif Nazrul
summary_en: At a 2 July 2025 ministry seminar on Japan's labour market, Expatriates' Welfare Adviser Asif Nazrul said the government process for sending workers abroad is deliberately complex and promised to simplify it for Japan, if necessary keeping no home-side official process. He said Bangladesh cannot meet Japan's demand because workers lack language and job skills, outlined a public-private training plan and possible student loans from Probashi Kallyan Bank, and an ILO adviser compared Bangladesh's 4 to 5 thousand a year to Japan with Nepal's 50,000-plus.

facts.statement: Expatriates' Welfare Adviser Asif Nazrul said the government process for sending manpower to overseas labour markets is complex and long, that such processes are kept to give some people jobs and to commit corruption, and that government work needs 10 to 12 signatures for no reason.

Asif Nazrul promised that for sending manpower to Japan the process will be made as simple as possible with everyone's advice, and if necessary no official process will be kept in Bangladesh: 'whatever has to be done, the Japanese will do'. He said sending people to Singapore had many weaknesses and questioned why so much checking from Bangladesh is needed for a country where everything is on record.

Asif Nazrul said going to Japan requires both language and job skills, whereas going to various Middle East countries needs no skill and not even the language; this is why more people go to the Middle East and Bangladesh cannot send people to Japan in line with demand, although Japan's demand for manpower will grow.

The adviser said the government is thinking of a public-private partnership (PPP) under which Japanese entrepreneurs come to Bangladesh, train people according to their own needs and take them, and of involving some credible, reliable Bangladeshi institutions in producing skilled manpower.

On student visas, Asif Nazrul said the problem is that a bank guarantee cannot be obtained; he said he would discuss a proposal with some private banks, and that introducing loans for students from Probashi Kallyan Bank would be discussed seriously.

Asif Nazrul said sending people to many countries has stopped because of the misdeeds and violent activities of a small number of workers; he said he had heard that in many countries people from Sylhet and Brahmanbaria regularly announce and fight each other, and that in one place in Saudi Arabia Bengali thugs attack other Bengalis to snatch and loot money. He said migrant workers must be aware of these things.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' Welfare Adviser Asif Nazrul (corrected quote per the article's correction note)

facts.statement: ILO policy adviser Zia Hassan said Nepal has increased its manpower exports to Japan every year since Covid: about 4 to 5 thousand people a year now go from Bangladesh to Japan, while more than 50,000 go from Nepal.
Over the next five years Japan has demand for eight and a quarter lakh (সোয়া আট লাখ) workers skilled in 16 specific types of work.

The Chief Adviser's special envoy for international affairs Lutfey Siddiqi said memoranda on manpower export have been signed many times before, and the government must think about working differently inside government to implement them; Asif Nazrul named lack of coordination among government offices and ministries and lack of accountability as the first problems.

The seminar 'New labour market in Japan: challenges of sending workers and what to do' was organised by the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry at the International Mother Language Institute auditorium, Segunbagicha, Dhaka; IOM Bangladesh chief of mission Lance Bonneau, senior secretary Neyamat Ullah Bhuiyan and recruiting agency owners attended.
